articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Sales of Bharat Rice have plunged sharply after the Centre withdrew the subsidy provided under the scheme, falling from around 14.6 lakh tonnes
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Sales of Bharat Rice have plunged sharply after the Centre withdrew the subsidy provided under the scheme, falling from around 14.6 lakh tonnes in its first phase in 2024 to just 82,088 tonnes in the third phase (July 2025-June 2026), an RTI reply has revealed.The subsidy, which was initially Rs 5.4 per kg, was reduced to Rs 2 per kg in the second phase before being completely withdrawn from July 2025. Govt has not provided any support from the Price Stabilisation Fund (PSF) since then.The information was disclosed by the food department in response to an RTI application filed by Kerala-based RTI activist K Govindan Nampoothiry.Launched on Feb 6, 2024, Bharat Rice was aimed at providing rice to consumers at subsidised rates under the Open Market Sale Scheme (Domestic). Food Corporation of India (FCI) sells excess stocks from the central pool through three cooperative organisations: NAFED, NCCF and Kendriya Bhandar.According to the reply, as against an allocation of 17.5 lakh tonnes in the first phase (Feb-June 2024), 14.6 lakh tonnes of rice were sold. Sales fell to 2.7 lakh tonnes in the second phase (July 2024-June 2025) compared with an allocation of 2.9 lakh tonnes. In the third phase (July 2025-June 2026), sales dropped further to 82,088 tonnes as against the 1.6 lakh tonnes allocated.The decline has continued in the ongoing fourth phase. articles.title: For many young people, the path to homeownership means moving in with parents
articles.summary: More than 1 in 5 of this year's first-time buyers reported living with parents, relatives, or friends immediately before buying a home, according to National...
articles.body:
As home prices and mortgage rates remain elevated, young people are trying a new tactic to accelerate their home savings: moving back in with mom and dad.

More than 1 in 5 of this year's first-time buyers reported living with parents, relatives, or friends immediately before buying a home, according to National Association of Realtors data, a level that jumped during the pandemic and has remained elevated in the years since. In the 1990s, as few as 12% of buyers had such an arrangement.

The uptick comes as a major hurdle to first-time homeownership — saving for a down payment — is getting harder. Higher home prices mean more money down, while rising rents eat into savings rates, slowing down the process. One study by the Center for Responsible Lending's Julian Bond Institute found that the time it takes a typical renter family to save for a down payment doubled from 8 to 16 years between 2019 and 2026.

The appeal of living at home is obvious: Housing costs are the single largest line item on most budgets, and parents are often happy to let their children live rent-free or at below-market rates.

"It's a great way to save up money," said Jeff Silver, a mortgage loan officer with Big Valley Mortgage in Roseville, Calif.

He counsels clients in rent-free living situations to make "pretend" mortgage payments straight into their savings accounts. In his area, where the median home lists for nearly $650,000, he rarely sees monthly home payments below $3,800. Saving that for a year would bring in over $45,000 and cover a down payment.

More young adults are living at home regardless of whether they're explicitly saving for a home. As of last year, roughly 1 in 3 adults under 35 lived with their parents, just off of all-time highs reached during the early days of the pandemic.

"I somewhat view it positively," Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist, said of young people who are living at home and stockpiling cash instead of renting. "A down payment is one of the major barriers to getting into that first level."

Young adults who choose to move back home to fast-track their savings are trading away some short-term independence in hopes of a healthy long-term financial future. And for parents or relatives looking for ways to help children get a foothold into an expensive market, offering up a spare bedroom can be a powerful alternative to a direct cash gift.

Ruthie Bult, 26, and her husband moved in with her parents in New Hampshire shortly after she gave birth to their now 1-year-old son. They had hoped to stay just a few months while hunting for a home nearby, but found little available inventory and a competitive market. They've now lived with her parents for almost a year.

articles.title: Trump wants to work with Democrats on placing 10 percent cap on credit card interest rates
articles.summary: President Trump reupped his call for a 10 percent cap on credit card interest rates, saying he would be willing to work with Democrats on the issue. “I didn’t even know they said it but they’ve been trying to get that for years. I would do it,” Trump said during a phone call interview with…
articles.body:
President Trump reupped his call for a 10 percent cap on credit card interest rates, saying he would be willing to work with Democrats on the issue.

“I didn’t even know they said it but they’ve been trying to get that for years. I would do it,” Trump said during a phone call interview with Fox News’ “Saturday in America.”

“These credit card companies have made a lot and the credit card fees that they charge,” the president added. “I know some people would say it’s not free enterprise, but what’s free enterprise when you’re sitting home and you get a bill that some guy set up in an office on Park Avenue and they say let’s charge a fee that’s too high.”

The president’s comments come as Americans are grappling with rising credit card balances. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported last week that credit card balances increased by $22 billion in the third quarter. This is a 1.7 percent increase from the second quarter.

This year, credit card debt surpassed $1.28 trillion with balances in the third quarter being $52 billion more than what they were one year ago. The average credit card interest rate as of Nov. 4 stands at 19.71 percent, according to Bankrate .

Democrats previously have called for the capping of credit card interest rates and so has the president.

On Nov. 8, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who is in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee, said she wants to codify that cap when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress in January

“I got the bill, I’m ready to go,” Warren said on CBS News’s “ Face the Nation ” earlier this month.

Texas’ incoming Democratic senator James Talarico has mentioned capping “sky-high” credit card interest rates in his campaign , vowing to “rein in the predatory credit card companies ripping people off.”

Earlier this year in January, Trump called for the placing a one-year cap on the credit card interest rates, saying, “we will no longer let the American Public be ‘ripped off’ by Credit Card Companies that are charging Interest Rates of 20 to 30%, and even more, which festered unimpeded during the Sleepy Joe Biden Administration. AFFORDABILITY!”
